transcript.text: I am the operations lead at a tour company. Each month I tell our local partners how many guides to reserve in each destination for the month after next. If I reserve too few, we hire freelancers at the last minute for about three times the price; if I reserve too many, we pay a small fee for each guide we do not use. My director asked me for a machine learning model that forecasts how many bookings we will receive per destination each month. The table I shared is our booking export up to late February 2026: one row per booking with the booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. I will use the result myself every month to fix the reservation. [shares bookings.csv]

Here's what I'm hearing, so I can correct you if I'm off: each month you need, **per destination, a number of guides to reserve for the month after next**. Over-reserving costs a small fee; under-reserving costs ~3× freelancer rates, so I'd bias the number slightly high.

Your table has that in it: 1,500 bookings across 6 destinations, booked Jan 2025–Feb 2026, with travel dates out to Aug 2026, and a `cancelled` flag. Good — I can anchor a real number.

The trap I'd avoid: predicting raw booking volume. What serves your decision is **expected non-cancelled travellers per destination per month**, timed by **travel_date** (not booking_date), forecast two months ahead.

The plan I'd run:
1. **Baseline first** — historical monthly travellers per destination plus cancellation, so we can see seasonality and give you a starting number even before any model.
2. **Features** — destination, month/season, lead time, channel, nationality, price, free-cancellation.
3. **Model** expected non-cancelled bookings per destination-month; check it on the most recent months as a holdout.
4. **Turn the forecast into a reservation count** using your asymmetric costs (aim slightly above the midpoint so under-reservation is the rare, expensive error).
5. **A monthly routine** — you drop in the latest export, get one number per destination.

Here are the routes, and the one your director named is the recommendation:

The three routes above are now in front of you. My read is that the **model** is what your director asked for and what serves your decision best — but note it rests on one thing I haven't pinned down: whether a booking is one traveller or a party of people. Your export is "one row per booking" — if a booking can cover 2–8 people, we'd need to count passengers, not rows, or every number will be too low.

Two small assumptions I'm making, tell me if they're wrong: a "guide" covers a set number of travellers per day (so a guide count, not a booking count, is the real target), and cancelling a guide you reserved costs that "small fee" — no penalty for cancelling a traveller's booking.

Which route would you like to start with?

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

You get: A monthly screen you open to see current demand per destination and decide the reservation by eye. transcript.text: I am the head of marketing at a subscription company. The board asked for an AI segmentation of our customers, and I would like five or six segments with names we can put on a slide. The table I shared has one row per customer: signup date, the segment we already record, city, plan, tenure in months, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. Next quarter my team can run at most three email campaigns: one to move people to a higher plan, one to keep people who look likely to leave, and one welcome series for new customers. The same person should not receive two of them. My campaign managers will use the segments to decide who gets which campaign. [shares customers.csv]

Your table confirms why the board wants this: the segment you record today only distinguishes consumer (961, 18.1% churn) from business (239, 14.6%) — too coarse for three different campaigns. The real job is to find five or six natural groups inside those 1,200 customers using tenure, spend, plan, support tickets and churn behaviour, name each one, and map each to at most one of your three campaigns (upgrade, retention, welcome) so nobody gets two. The obvious route — renaming the two existing segments — can't do that; unsupervised groups on the behavioural columns can.

Here's the approach I'd take, in steps: 1) profile the 1,200 rows on the behavioural columns (tenure, spend, plan, support tickets) to make sure the groups that emerge are real, not noise. 2) build the segmentation and hold back a sample to check the groups are stable and behave differently on churn. 3) name each segment in plain board language and write its one-line profile. 4) map each segment to at most one of your three campaigns, with the rule that a person in two candidate segments gets the more urgent one (retention before upgrade, upgrade before welcome). 5) hand your campaign managers a named-segment table plus the assignment rule, ready for the slide.

Two ways to start — the segmentation build directly, or the quick campaign-pool numbers first to sanity-check the board's three-campaign plan. Pick one, or just tell me to build the segmentation and I'll get it going.

You get: A slide-ready table: 5–6 named segments, who they are, and which of your three campaigns each maps to — one campaign per person. Your campaign managers get the rule for who is in each group. Trade-off: It is a model build: DCLab splits the data, checks the groups on a holdout before you see names, so you get the result after one build cycle, not instantly. Effort: Medium — one build, reviewed before you take it to the board.

transcript.text: I am the credit risk manager at a consumer lender that finances phone and appliance purchases in shops. Today a rulebook written by our underwriters approves about 40 percent of applications. Management wants to grow, so they asked me for a machine learning model that predicts default for every applicant, to replace the rulebook and approve more people safely. We have about 60,000 past loans with the application form, the bureau score and whether the loan defaulted within 12 months, and I can export them next week. For the applications we rejected we kept the form and the bureau score, nothing more. The model would decide each new application automatically at the shop counter. How should I go about it?

Here's how I'd frame the problem and the path.

The real problem isn't "train a model" — it's that your outcomes only exist for the 40% the rulebook already approved. That's the trap that sinks most rulebook-replacement projects: the model learns risk inside the approved population, and the people you want to newly approve are exactly the ones it has never seen default. The honest answer is a model trained on the 60,000 approved loans, anchored hard on the bureau score (which you *do* have for rejections, so you can see how far below today's bar you're going), plus a deliberate decision about how far to trust the model outside its training range — that decision usually deserves a small experiment, not just an extrapolation.

My plan, once the data is in:

1. **Ingest and sanity-check** your export next week: default base rate, bureau score distribution for approved vs rejected, and a leakage check (drop anything written after the loan was made).
2. **Baseline the rulebook**: current approval rate, default rate of approved loans, and how much the bureau score alone separates good from bad. No model beats that gets replaced.
3. **Train a gradient-boosted model** on the approved loans, form fields plus bureau score, with a holdout it has never seen. I'll check accuracy and calibration, not just ranking.
4. **Backtest against your goal**: simulate the model at different cutoffs — you'll see the trade-off curve of "approve X% more" against "default rate rises to Y%". That curve is what management is actually deciding.
5. **Handle the rejected zone**: use the rejections' scores to see how much of the newly-approved population is extrapolation, and decide between extending by score band or running a short randomized-approval pilot on borderline applicants to learn their true default rate.

The one number I still need from you later: what default rate management accepts at the higher approval level — that sets the cutoff. For now, share the export next week and I'll start with step 1.

transcript.text: I am the operations lead at a tour company. Each month I tell our local partners how many guides to reserve in each destination for the month after next. If I reserve too few, we hire freelancers at the last minute for about three times the price; if I reserve too many, we pay a small fee for each guide we do not use. My director asked me for a machine learning model that forecasts how many bookings we will receive per destination each month. The table I shared is our booking export up to late February 2026: one row per booking with the booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. I will use the result myself every month to fix the reservation. [shares bookings.csv]

# Forecasting Guide Reservations by Destination

## 1. The problem, stated plainly

**The decision.** Each month you pick, for every destination, an integer: the number of guides to lock in with the local partner for the travel month two months ahead. That single number is the output you hand to the partner.

**Who uses it and when.** You, the operations lead, make this call yourself on a monthly cadence. The director's "ML model" is a means to your end; the deliverable you actually need is a per-destination number you can defend and act on. The decision is made in month *t*, the guides serve month *t + 2*, and the cost is settled in *t + 2*.

**The unit of analysis.** One destination, one travel-month. The 1,500-row table gives you booking-level history; the forecast must be aggregated up to (destination × month).

**What you know.**
- 1,500 booking rows, each with booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time (days), a price field (stored as categorical, likely price tiers), free-cancellation flag, and a cancelled flag.
- The data is current through late February 2026.
- The cost asymmetry: an unfilled guide slot is roughly free (small fixed fee per unused guide); a shortage forces a freelancer at about three times the contracted rate. You did not give me the absolute amounts, only the ratio and the qualitative direction.
- You will be the sole consumer of the forecast; there is no downstream system that ingests a probability distribution.

**What is not known and you should check before starting.**
- The time span of the export (does it cover two years or three months? This changes everything).
- How many distinct destinations appear, and how bookings are spread across them.
- Whether one booking maps to one guide, or whether group bookings need a single guide, or whether a guide covers multiple bookings per day.
- What the "price" column actually encodes (price tier? currency? a product variant?).
- Whether the small excess fee is truly negligible relative to the 3× freelancer premium, or whether it is large enough to shift the optimum noticeably.
- Whether partner contracts impose a minimum reservation or a rounding rule (e.g., reserve in blocks of 5).

---

## 2. Approaches on the table, with what each costs and gives

| # | Approach | What it does | Cost / effort | What you get | Where it breaks |
|---|----------|-------------|---------------|--------------|----------------|
| A | **No model: seasonal average + already-booked head-start** | For each destination, take the historical mean of *non-cancelled* bookings in month *M* (adjusted for month-of-year), then add the bookings already visible in your export whose travel date falls in *M*. Cap or floor with a simple rule. | Hours to build in a spreadsheet. Re-runs each month in minutes. | Transparent number you can explain to the director in one sentence. Captures the most important effect: "some April bookings are already in the system." | Ignores trend, new destinations, channel mix shifts, and cancellation drift. Treats every month as interchangeable within a season. |
| B | **Booking-lead-time curve + cancellation survival** | Model *when* bookings arrive relative to travel date (the lead-time distribution per destination/season), and *whether* a booked guest cancels. For the target month, project how many additional bookings will land before the travel window closes, net of expected cancellations. This is a small statistical model (e.g., a Beta or Poisson fit on lead-time, a logistic on cancellation). | A few days in Python/R. Needs the full history; works even if a destination has only a dozen observations because you can pool across destinations and add a destination-level offset. | Separates the two processes that actually drive your number (arrival of new bookings, survival against cancellation). Gives you a *range*, not just a point, so you can see the downside. | Still assumes the lead-time and cancellation patterns you saw historically will hold. Needs at least a season or two of history to be stable. |
| C | **Supervised ML (gradient-boosted trees, e.g., LightGBM)** on booking-level features to predict per-destination monthly non-cancelled count. | You frame it as: given features observable at decision time (month of year, channel mix so far, lead-time profile, free-cancellation share, price tier mix, nationality mix, destination), predict the final non-cancelled count for that destination-month. Train on past destination-months; test on holdout. | A week or two of feature engineering + tuning. 1,500 rows is at the low end for a tree ensemble, especially once you slice by destination. You will fight overfitting. | Captures non-linear interactions (e.g., "German guests on the OTA channel book 90 days out and cancel less in summer"). Gives feature-importance you can show the director. | With 1,500 rows and possibly a handful of destinations, you risk a model that memorises noise. The "ML" label satisfies the director but the operational value over approach B is small. Harder to explain *why* April needs 12 guides and not 9. |
| D | **Newsvendor / stochastic inventory** layered on top of any forecast from A–C. | You already have a demand estimate (point + spread). The reservation question is a classic newsvendor: choose *Q* to minimise E[cost] = (shortage probability × 3× rate) + (surplus × small fee). Closed-form if you assume a normal or Gamma demand; a simple loop otherwise. | Hours once you have the forecast. The formula is two lines. | Turns a forecast into the *actual decision number* in a way that respects the 3× vs small-fee asymmetry. This is where the business value lives, and it is the piece the director's "forecast model" brief skips. | Needs a defensible spread (variance) on the forecast, which approach A gives you poorly. |

---

## 3. What I would do, and in what order

I would **not** build approach C first. With 1,500 rows, the tree model will overfit, and the operational gain over B is marginal. The director asked for "a machine learning model," but the thing that actually protects the company's margin is the newsvendor step (D) sitting on a transparent, checkable forecast (B). I would frame the deliverable to the director as a *forecasting and optimisation pipeline* that happens to use a small statistical model, and reserve the tree-based version as a v2 once you have two or more years of clean history.

### Step-by-step plan

**Step 0 – Data audit (½ day).**
- Confirm the date span, the number of destinations, and the booking-to-guide mapping.
- Check the `price` column: if it is a tier label, keep it; if it is a mis-typed numeric, fix it.
- Verify that `cancelled` is truly 0/1 and that `lead_time_days` is consistent with `travel_date − booking_date`.
- Flag any destination with fewer than, say, a handful of historical travel-months; those will need the pooled estimate.
*You need from me:* the raw file and a one-paragraph note on the guide-to-booking rule and the two cost figures.

**Step 1 – Build the "already on the books" count (½ day).**
- For the target travel month (month *t + 2*), pull every row in the export whose `travel_date` falls in that month and whose `cancelled` = 0. Group by destination. This is the floor of your forecast: these guests are already committed (subject to future cancellation, which Step 2 handles).
*Check:* does this number look sane compared to last year's same month?

**Step 2 – Model the arrival of *new* bookings and cancellation survival (2–3 days).**
- **Arrival:** for each destination (pooling across destinations if any is sparse), fit the empirical lead-time distribution of *bookings that ultimately did not cancel*. The question you answer: "Given it is now month *t*, and travel is *t + 2*, how many more bookings do I expect to see arrive before travel, based on the lead-time curve?" This is a simple CDF / survival lookup, or a small Poisson rate if you prefer.
- **Cancellation survival:** fit a logistic (or just compute the historical cancel rate by destination, free-cancellation flag, and channel) to estimate the fraction of already-booked and newly-arriving bookings that will still be standing at travel time.
- Combine: *expected final demand* = (already-booked × survival) + (expected new arrivals × survival for new bookings).
- Record the *variance* (or a 10th–90th percentile band) from the residual scatter, because Step 3 needs it.
*Check:* replay the model for three or four past months you know the answer to (walk-forward). If the prediction is off by more than a guide or two in the majority of replayed months, the model is not ready and you should widen the band or fall back to approach A's seasonal average.

**Step 3 – Newsvendor optimisation (½ day).**
- Input: the point forecast and the spread from Step 2, the 3× freelancer rate, the small excess fee, and any partner minimum/rounding rule.
- Compute the critical fractile: *F(Q\*) = (cost of one short) / (cost of one short + cost of one excess)*. With a 3× premium and a small excess fee, this fractile will be high (you are biased toward over-reserving slightly), which matches your intuition that a small fee is cheap insurance.
- Read off *Q\*** from the demand distribution. That integer is the number you send to the partner.
- Also produce the two "what-if" numbers: what you pay if demand hits the 10th percentile, and what you pay if it hits the 90th.
*Check:* run the same calculation with last month's actuals as a back-test. The expected cost of the recommended *Q\** should be at or below the expected cost of last month's actual reservation.

**Step 4 – Operationalise the monthly run (1 day).**
- Wrap Steps 1–3 in a script (Python or R) that you re-run on a fixed date each month (e.g., the 1st of month *t*) once the booking export is refreshed.
- Output: a one-page table – destination, already-booked, expected arrivals, expected final demand, recommended reservation, 10th/90th percentiles, expected cost.
- You copy that table into the partner e-mail.
- Log the actual outcome each month so you have a running back-test log.

**Step 5 – Review and stop criteria.**
- After three months of live use, compare recommended vs. actual demand and the realised cost.
- **Stop and iterate** if: (a) the 90th-percentile band is consistently violated in the same direction (the model is miscalibrated); (b) a new destination appears that has no history (use the pooled estimate until it accumulates its own data); (c) the partner changes the fee structure or the freelancer rate.
- **Stop and switch to approach C** (the tree model) only when you have at least two full seasons of data *and* the simple model is still off by a guide or more in a meaningful fraction of months. At 1,500 rows you do not yet meet that bar.

---

## 4. What I took from you vs. what I am assuming

**From you, stated plainly:** 1,500-row export through late Feb 2026; the columns listed; the 3× freelancer penalty; a "small fee" for unused guides; you are the sole user; the decision cadence is monthly for the month after next; the director framed it as an ML forecast.

**I am assuming (please confirm or correct):**
- One booking corresponds to one guide-day, or there is a fixed small group size. If guides cover multiple bookings or if there is a group-size column I should look for, the aggregation changes.
- The "small fee" is small enough that the newsvendor fractile sits well above 0.5 (i.e., you are incentivised to lean toward over-reserving). If the fee is actually comparable to a fraction of the guide cost, the optimum shifts and I would need the real number.
- The booking-to-guide mapping does not depend on nationality, channel, or price tier.
- The lead-time distribution and cancellation rate are roughly stable month-to-month within a season; there is no one-off event (pandemic, visa rule change, partner going out of business) embedded in the history that would distort the curve.
- The 1,500 rows span more than a few months; if they only cover, say, October 2025 to February 2026, the seasonal estimate in Step 2 has very little to work with and I would lean harder on the pooled, month-of-year average (approach A) and widen the uncertainty band accordingly.

If any of those assumptions is wrong, tell me which one and I will adjust the plan before we touch the data.

## What the problem actually is

The board's ask ("AI segmentation, five or six named segments for a slide") is the *frame*, but the decision it serves is more concrete: **assign each of the 1,200 customers to at most one of three mutually-exclusive campaigns next quarter** — upgrade-pitch, retention-save, or new-customer welcome — and leave the rest untouched. The campaign managers are the day-to-day users of the output; the board is the one-time audience for the story. The unit is one customer row, and the moment is *next quarter*, a forward-looking window.

What is known from your description: the table has 1,200 rows, one per customer, with an identifier, a signup date, an existing internal "segment" label, city, plan, tenure in months, monthly spend, a 90-day support-ticket count, and a 0/1 flag for whether the customer churned the following month. You can run at most three campaigns, and no customer may receive two.

What is *not* known, and where I have to assume:

- I do not know the values or cardinality of the existing "segment" column, "city," or "plan." I assume each has a modest number of levels (say, fewer than ten) so they can be treated as categorical predictors rather than high-cardinality noise.
- I assume "churned_next_month" is binary (0 or 1) and that it records an *observed* outcome from the data's historical window, not a prediction for the coming quarter.
- I assume "support_tickets_90d" is a small non-negative integer (0, 1, 2, …).
- I assume "plan" has an inherent ordering (e.g., Basic → Pro → Enterprise) so that "higher plan" is well-defined.
- I assume "monthly_spend" and "tenure_months" are continuous enough to be split at meaningful thresholds.

The tension to keep in front of you: the board wants a picture that *looks* like the product of an algorithm; the managers need groups they can act on with a clear, explainable rule; and the three campaigns have a natural priority (a new customer is not also an at-risk customer, and an at-risk customer should not be upsold). Those three needs pull in different directions, and the solution has to honour all three.

---

## Approaches on the table

**A. Pure rule-based segmentation (no statistical model).**
You (with the campaign managers) set a handful of thresholds — "tenure below X months → New," "lowest plan tier + spend in the top quartile → Upgrade Candidate," "high ticket count + low spend → At-Risk," and so on — and hand-name the resulting five or six groups.
*Cost:* a one-day workshop with the managers; no code beyond a simple `if/else` or a `CASE` statement.
*Gives:* instantly board-readable names; the mapping from segment → campaign is explicit and auditable; the managers can explain to a customer why they got a particular email.
*Does not give:* you are not "letting the data speak"; if your thresholds are off, the segments are off, and you have no principled way to know. The board may see "AI" and expect something more.

**B. Unsupervised clustering (k-means, Gaussian mixture, or hierarchical) on the numeric and encoded categorical features.**
Standardise the numeric columns, one-hot or frequency-encode the categoricals, run a clusterer for *k* = 5 or 6, then name the clusters after inspecting their centroid profiles.
*Cost:* moderate — a few hours of feature engineering and a short tuning session (choosing *k*, checking silhouette scores, making sure no cluster is a singleton).
*Gives:* data-driven groupings that may reveal natural sub-populations (e.g., "long-tenure, low-spend, high-ticket" as a distinct group). The "AI" story is credible.
*Does not give:* clean operational mapping. A cluster might contain people who are both new and at-risk, muddying the "no customer gets two campaigns" rule. Names are retrospective and can sound jargony on a slide. You also have to decide whether to include "churned_next_month" as a feature (leakage risk if you then use the cluster for a forward decision) or leave it out (in which case the "At-Risk" segment is not directly data-grounded).

**C. Supervised churn model + rule-based carve-out (hybrid).**
Train a short, interpretable classifier (logistic regression or a shallow gradient-boosted tree) to predict "churned_next_month" from the other columns. Use the predicted probability to carve out a genuine "At-Risk" segment. Then apply simple business rules (tenure, plan tier, spend band) to split the remaining customers into the other four or five segments.
*Cost:* a day or two to build and validate the churn model (cross-validation on the 1,200 rows), plus the rule workshop from approach A.
*Gives:* the one segment that matters most to the board — "who will leave" — is grounded in a real model, which satisfies the "AI" ask without over-claiming. The other segments are explainable, and the three campaigns fall out of the rules in a mutually-exclusive order. You can put the model's accuracy or the area under the ROC curve on a small appendix slide for credibility.
*Does not give:* you are relying on a historical label to say something about next quarter. If your customer base or your product changed materially, the model's ranking may not transfer. Also, 1,200 rows is small; the model will be noisy, and you should be transparent about that.

**D. Use the existing "segment" column as-is and add at most one or two splits.**
If the company already records, say, "New / Active / Lapsed / VIP," you simply refine: split "Active" by spend into "Active-Low" and "Active-High," add a "At-Risk" flag from the ticket count, and stop.
*Cost:* minimal — a spreadsheet pivot and a naming session.
*Gives:* continuity with what the rest of the company already tracks; zero modelling.
*Does not give:* it will not read as "AI" to the board, and you are not using the numerical columns (spend, tenure, tickets) to their full potential.

---

## What I would choose and why

**Approach C — the hybrid (supervised churn model for the risk segment + rule-based splits for the rest) — is the best fit for this specific decision.**

Rationale in one sentence: the board needs *one* defensible "AI" artefact on the slide (the churn model and its output segment), while the managers need the other four or five segments to be *actionable* and *explainable* (rules, not cluster centroids), and the mutual-exclusivity constraint is cleanest when the three campaigns are assigned in a fixed, ordered priority.

---

## The plan, step by step

**Step 1 – Clean and profile the data (half a day, you or an analyst).**
- Confirm 1,200 rows, no duplicate "customer_id," no missing values in the columns you will use.
- Look at the distributions of "tenure_months," "monthly_spend," and "support_tickets_90d" (histograms, quartiles). Note where natural breaks appear.
- List the distinct values of "plan" and confirm the ordering. List the distinct values of the existing "segment" and "city."
- Check the overall rate of "churned_next_month = 1." If it is extremely imbalanced (say, well under 5 %), flag it now because it affects how you build the churn model in Step 2.
*What you need:* the raw CSV, a notebook or spreadsheet. *How you check it:* you can eyeball the distributions and the value lists; no model yet.

**Step 2 – Build and validate the churn model (one day).**
- Target: "churned_next_month." Features: "tenure_months," "monthly_spend," "support_tickets_90d," "plan" (ordinal-encoded), "signup_date" (convert to days-since-signup, or drop it if "tenure_months" already captures it), "city" and "segment" (frequency-encoded or dropped if they add little).
- Model: start with logistic regression (interpretable coefficients, easy to explain on a slide); if you want a little more flexibility, a gradient-boosted tree with shallow trees (depth ≤ 4) is fine. Do not reach for deep learning or ensembles of dozens of trees — 1,200 rows will not support them, and the board will not follow the explanation.
- Validation: 5-fold cross-validation. Report the area under the ROC curve and the precision at a "top 20 %" threshold (i.e., of the 20 % of customers you flag as highest-risk, how many actually churned in the historical window). Be honest in the deck: this is a *historical* hit rate, not a guarantee for next quarter.
*What you need:* the cleaned data, a Python or R session, roughly an hour of compute. *How you check it:* the CV metrics, a confusion matrix at the threshold you choose, and a sanity check that the model is not just ranking by one variable (e.g., it should not simply say "everyone with 3+ tickets is at risk" without the other features contributing). *When to stop:* when the ROC AUC is stable across folds and you can articulate in one sentence why a given customer is in the "At-Risk" group. If the AUC is near 0.5 (no better than a coin flip), go back to Step 1 and check whether the features actually carry signal; do not force a model.

**Step 3 – Set the business rules for the remaining segments (a one-hour workshop with the three campaign managers).**
Using the distributions from Step 1, agree on:
- A **tenure cutoff** that separates "new" from "established" customers. (You will pick the number from the data's natural break; I am not going to guess it for you.)
- A **plan tier** that defines "eligible for upgrade" (e.g., the customer is not already on the top tier, or is on the bottom tier).
- A **spend band** (e.g., top quartile of "monthly_spend" among non-new customers) that identifies "high-value" customers.
- A **ticket-count threshold** above which a customer is "service-stressed" (this can double as a secondary check on the churn model).

These rules, combined with the churn model's flag, give you five to six segments. As an illustrative *logic* (the actual names and thresholds come from your workshop):

| Segment (name on the slide) | How it is defined (logic) | Campaign next quarter |
|---|---|---|
| 1. New & Enthusiastic | Tenure below the cutoff; not flagged at-risk | Welcome series |
| 2. New & Wary | Tenure below the cutoff; high tickets or flagged at-risk | Retention-save (take priority over welcome) |
| 3. Loyal High-Value | Established tenure; top spend band; not at-risk | Upgrade-pitch (if not on top plan) or *no campaign* (if on top plan) |
| 4. Established & Steady | Established tenure; middle spend; not at-risk | *No campaign* (maintenance) |
| 5. Service-Stressed / At-Risk | Flagged by the churn model or ticket count above threshold, regardless of tenure | Retention-save |
| 6. Value Upgrade Candidates | Established tenure; on a lower plan tier; spend in the upper portion; not at-risk | Upgrade-pitch |

The exact count (five or six) and the names will come out of the workshop. The key structural rule: **assign in priority order — (1) new-customer welcome, (2) at-risk / retention, (3) upgrade — and stop the moment a customer is assigned.** That guarantees no one receives two campaigns. Customers who fall into none of the three campaign-eligible segments simply get no email this quarter.

**Step 4 – Build the assignment table and the slide (half a day).**
- Produce a one-row-per-customer output: "customer_id," segment name, assigned campaign (or "none").
- Verify: no "customer_id" appears under two campaigns. Confirm the counts add to 1,200.
- For the slide: one slide with the five or six segment names, a short one-line description of each, the approximate count of customers in each, and the campaign arrow. A small appendix note: "The At-Risk segment was identified by a logistic-regression model (ROC AUC = [value], 5-fold CV, trained on [period] historical churn)."
*How you check it:* a quick cross-tab of segment × campaign; a `COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)` per campaign to confirm the cap of three is met and no overlap. *When to stop:* when the counts reconcile to 1,200, no ID appears twice, and the three managers each point at their campaign's rows and say "yes, that's the right group."

**Step 5 – Brief the campaign managers and the board (the meetings).**
- With the managers: walk through the rules, the thresholds you chose, and any boundary cases (a customer who is both new and at-risk goes to retention, not welcome — confirm they are comfortable with that priority).
- With the board: present the slide. Pre-empt the "is this really AI?" question by naming the model and its validation metric in one line, and pre-empt the "what happens after the campaign?" question by noting that the segmentation is a *snapshot* for next quarter and will need to be re-run when new signup and spend data come in.

**You told me:** the table's shape (1,200 rows, the nine columns listed), the three campaigns and their mutual-exclusivity rule, that the board wants five or six named segments on a slide, that the campaign managers are the operational users, and that the decision horizon is next quarter.

**I am assuming (state them if they are wrong and I will adjust):**
- "churned_next_month" is a binary 0/1 *observed* label from a historical window, not a forward prediction.
- "plan" has a natural tier ordering (low → high).
- "support_tickets_90d" is a small non-negative integer.
- "city" and the existing "segment" have modest cardinality (well under a few dozen levels).

I am a data scientist at a company that sells accounting software to small firms. Two years ago we built a model that scores every new lead on how likely it is to become a customer, and the sales team calls the highest scores first. Since the autumn the sales team says the top leads are much worse than they used to be, and my manager wants me to retrain with a larger model and more features. Some context on the data: since the summer, part of our leads comes from a partner marketplace; we moved to a new CRM in August, and two form fields the model uses are no longer collected; and finance now counts a lead as converted when a free trial starts, where before it was the first payment. I have the old training set and every lead since, not yet exported. What would you do?

# What's actually going on, and what I'd do

## The problem in plain terms

The decision the model serves is *which leads the sales team calls first, so that a finite number of calls produce the most conversions.* The user is the sales rep picking from a ranked list each morning; the unit is one lead (a small-firm account); the moment that matters is the instant a lead arrives and gets a score, and the moment a lead is labelled "converted" for training purposes.

What you **know**:

- A model built ~2 years ago scores leads; sales dials top scores first.
- Four things changed in roughly the same window: a new lead source (partner marketplace) appeared in summer; a new CRM went live in August; two form fields the model consumes stopped being collected; and finance redefined "converted" from *first payment* to *free-trial start*.
- You hold the old training set and every lead record since, but they haven't been exported yet.

What you **do not know** (and this is the crux):

- Whether the top-scored leads are *actually* converting at a lower rate, or whether the sales team's perception is being skewed by the new source's volume, the CRM's different ranking display, or the easier trial-start label making the old payment-based scores look miscalibrated.
- How much of the two missing fields' predictive signal is truly gone versus recoverable.
- Whether the partner-marketplace leads are a genuinely different population or just a different channel into the same population.
- The size, feature set, and model type of the current system; the monthly lead volume; the actual conversion rates before and after.

Your manager's instinct—"retrain with a bigger model and more features"—treats this as a *capacity* problem. It almost certainly is not. What has happened is that the model is now being asked to answer a **different question** (trial-start vs. payment), with **missing inputs** (two fields), on a **shifted population** (new source), through a **different pipeline** (new CRM). No amount of model complexity fixes a mis-specified target, a null column, or a distribution shift.

---

## Approaches on the table, with their costs and what each gives you

| Approach | What it gives you | What it costs / risks |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Verify before touching the model.** Export the leads, pull outcomes under the *new* label, and compare top-decile conversion now vs. the historical baseline. | A clear, quantified diagnosis: is the problem the model, the data, the label, or the source mix? Cheap (a few analyst-days). | Slight delay before any "fix." Risk: findings are awkward for the "just retrain" narrative. |
| **B. Patch the data pipeline first, keep the model.** Recover or proxy the two missing fields, clean the CRM migration, tag source, then re-score with the existing model. | Fast, low-risk; tells you whether the model still works once inputs are sane. | If the target definition has genuinely shifted, the model is still answering the old question. |
| **C. Retrain on the cleaned, re-labelled data with the same model family.** | Directly addresses the label change and the source shift. Moderate effort. | Doesn't help if the data is still dirty or the target is still ambiguous. "Larger model" adds no value if the problem is specification, not capacity. |
| **D. Retrain with a *larger* model and *more* features (manager's ask).** | Marginal lift *if* and only if the current model is underfitting on a well-specified, clean dataset. | You'd be scaling up to solve a problem that isn't capacity. Costs engineering time, compute, and maintenance. Risks overfitting on a smaller post-change sample. |
| **E. Drop the model; go to rules or manual triage while you fix things.** | Guarantees the sales team isn't dialing on garbage scores. | Loses the personalisation you had; sales team morale hit; only a stopgap. |
| **F. Do nothing, accept the drift.** | Zero cost. | Pipeline degrades; revenue leakage; the problem compounds. Not defensible. |

No single approach is the whole answer, but *order* matters a lot.

---

## What I'd actually do, step by step

### Step 1 – Verify and diagnose (≈ 1–2 weeks, mostly your time + a DBA)

**What you need:** the exported lead records (old training set + every lead since the changes), the *new* conversion label (trial-start) applied consistently, and the old label (payment) for the pre-change window.

**Do:**

- Pull, for each lead: score, source (organic / partner marketplace / other), the two formerly-collected fields (now null or absent), CRM-migration flag, and outcome under **both** definitions of conversion.
- Split the timeline: *pre-change* (before ~July) and *post-change* (after).
- Compute, in each window: conversion rate in the top decile of scores, the overall AUC, the calibration curve (score vs. realised conversion).
- Separately, look at the partner-marketplace slice: does it convert at a structurally lower base rate, or does it just score low?
- Check the two missing fields: how predictive were they in the old model (feature-importance or ablation)? If they carried little weight, the "missing field" story is less damaging than it sounds.
- Check the CRM migration for data-quality artefacts: dropped fields, changed encodings, timestamp shifts that misalign the label window.

**Deliverable to your manager:** a one-page note: "The top-decile conversion rate dropped from X% to Y%. Z% of the gap is explained by the label change, W% by the new source, V% by missing fields, and the rest by the model. Here is the evidence." This re-frames the conversation from "build a bigger model" to "fix the specification."

**Stop condition:** if the diagnosis shows the top-decile rate is *not* materially worse (within normal weekly variance), you stop here and talk the sales team out of a false alarm. If it is worse, you continue.

### Step 2 – Agree on the business target (≈ 1 week, with your manager + sales lead + finance)

This is a *business* decision, not a modelling one:

- Does the sales team need to know "will this lead start a trial" (easier, more leads qualify) or "will this lead pay" (harder, the old question)? The answer should follow the sales rep's actual job: are they qualified to close a trial, or to close a payment?
- If finance counts a trial as a conversion for *reporting*, that does not automatically make it the right *optimisation target* for a scoring model.
- Decide whether you want one model or two (one for trial-start, one for payment), or a two-stage model (score for trial, then among trial-starters score for payment).

**Deliverable:** a written one-liner: "The model predicts *<target>* for a *<lead population>* within *<time horizon>*." Everyone signs off.

### Step 3 – Fix the data pipeline (≈ 2–4 weeks, with your engineers)

- **Missing fields:** can they be re-collected? If not, can you build proxies (e.g., derive company size from the marketplace profile, or use the CRM's new fields)? If a proxy is weak, *drop the feature* and accept the small information loss rather than feeding nulls.
- **Source tagging:** add a categorical "lead source" field to every record. If the partner marketplace feeds different fields, either map them to the common schema or keep a source-specific feature block.
- **CRM migration:** audit that every record since August has the fields it should; fix or flag the gaps.
- **Label window:** confirm that the "converted" label is stamped at the right moment (trial-start event, not form-submit, not some downstream finance entry) and that the observation window (how long after the lead you wait before calling it a non-conversion) is consistent.

**Deliverable:** a clean, versioned dataset: one row per lead, all features present (or explicitly null-and-dropped), source tagged, target labelled per the agreed definition, with a train/validation/test split that respects time (train on the past, validate on the most recent 4–6 weeks of post-change leads).

**Stop condition:** if the data can't be made clean enough (e.g., the partner source feeds 60% of the volume and its fields are fundamentally incompatible), you may need to scope the model to the sources you *can* score well and route the rest to a simple rule or manual review.

### Step 4 – Retrain (≈ 1–2 weeks)

- Use the **same model family** you had before (likely a gradient-boosted tree or a logistic model) unless Step 1 showed clear underfitting. "Bigger" is not the default answer. A well-specified small model on clean data will beat an under-specified big model on dirty data.
- Include *source* as a feature (or, if the partner leads are a structurally different population, train a separate model for them).
- Feature set: what's available post-fix. Don't add features you can't reliably collect; "more features" that are missing 40% of the time will hurt more than help.
- Train on the full history (both the old set and the new leads), but **weight or subsample** the old leads so the model doesn't over-index on the old label definition. In practice, you may simply re-label the entire history under the new definition and discard the old training set's labels.

**Deliverable:** a new model artifact, a feature list, a one-page model card (target, features, known limitations, expected AUC).

### Step 5 – Validate and shadow-deploy (≈ 2–4 weeks)

- **Offline:** on the held-out recent validation set, check AUC, top-decile lift (does the top 10% of new scores convert at a higher rate than the population average?), and calibration. Compare against the *old* model's scores on the same set.
- **Shadow / A-B:** run the new model in parallel with the old one for 2–4 weeks. Score every lead with both; log which score the sales team acted on (or randomly assign). Compare realised top-decile conversion.
- **Sanity checks:** score a handful of leads by hand with the sales team; does the new ranking *feel* right? Score leads from the partner marketplace separately and confirm they aren't systematically buried or inflated.

**Stop condition:** the new model's top-decile conversion rate is at or above the pre-change baseline, and the shadow test confirms no regression. If it's still below, you go back to diagnosis—don't iterate the model blindly.

### Step 6 – Monitor and maintain (ongoing)

- Weekly dashboard: score distribution, conversion rate by source, feature-missing rate, AUC on a rolling 2-week window.
- Alert if any of those drift beyond a set band.
- Re-evaluate the model quarterly or whenever another source / CRM / field change lands.
- Document the *label definition* in the model card so the next person doesn't inherit this ambiguity.

---

## What I'd push back on

- **"Larger model and more features" as the first response.** The evidence you have (four simultaneous changes) points to a *specification and data* problem, not a capacity problem. Scaling up the model before fixing the inputs, the label, and the population is building a bigger house on a cracked foundation. If, *after* steps 1–3, you have a clean, well-defined dataset and the current model family is genuinely underfitting, *then* a more complex model is a reasonable next experiment. But it's not the default.

- **Retraining before the data is clean.** You'd be baking the CRM artefacts, the nulls, and the mixed label definitions into the training set. The model would "learn" the noise.

- **Treating the label change as a bookkeeping detail.** Trial-start and first-payment are different events with different populations. A lead that starts a trial may never pay; a lead that pays skipped the trial. Scoring "will they pay" but labelling "did they start a trial" (or vice-versa) is a silent, systematic mis-label that no amount of model complexity fixes.

---

## One assumption I'm making

I'm assuming the two missing form fields can either be recovered, proxied, or safely dropped within a few weeks. If they are *irreplaceable* (e.g., a field that captured a competitor-in-use flag and the CRM migration destroyed it with no backup), the model's ceiling on those leads is permanently lower, and the right move is to accept the reduced signal rather than to pretend it's still there. You'd find out in Step 1, and it would change how much weight you put on the "fix the data" step vs. the "redefine what we can score" step.

Everything else above follows from what you told me. The numbers I'd need (conversion rates, lead volume, feature importance, sample sizes) will come out of Step 1, and I'd want them before I'd commit to any modelling choice.

I am the credit risk manager at a consumer lender that finances phone and appliance purchases in shops. Today a rulebook written by our underwriters approves about 40 percent of applications. Management wants to grow, so they asked me for a machine learning model that predicts default for every applicant, to replace the rulebook and approve more people safely. We have about 60,000 past loans with the application form, the bureau score and whether the loan defaulted within 12 months, and I can export them next week. For the applications we rejected we kept the form and the bureau score, nothing more. The model would decide each new application automatically at the shop counter. How should I go about it?

# The problem, stated plainly

**The decision.** For each walk-in applicant at the shop counter, decide *approve* or *decline* the financing before the customer walks away. Today that decision is a hand-written rulebook; you want a model to make it.

**Who uses the result.** Three people, in sequence. The salesperson sees only "yes / no / amount approved" in real time. You, the credit risk manager, set and monitor the threshold that turns the model's probability into that yes/no. Management reads the aggregate: approval rate, expected loss per portfolio, portfolio growth. If a regulator or internal audit asks why a particular applicant was declined, the explanation has to be traceable.

**Unit and moment.** One loan application, scored in the seconds-to-a-minute window the customer is at the counter. Not a batch at month-end.

**What you have told me you know.**
- ~60,000 *approved* loans from the past, each with the application form fields, the bureau score, and whether that borrower defaulted within 12 months.
- The rejected applications, with the same form fields and bureau score, but **no outcome** — because the loan never existed.
- The current rulebook, which approves roughly 40 % of applications.
- You can export the data next week.

**What you do not know (and what makes this hard).**
- The risk of the rejected population. You have their features but never observed whether they would have defaulted. A model trained only on the 60,000 approved loans has never seen a "bad" person look; it has learned to rank *among borrowers who already passed the rulebook*. If you simply lower the threshold or swap in that model, you will systematically underprice the risk of people who look like historical rejections, and the "approve more safely" goal will fail.
- The loss given default (how much of the financed phone or appliance is actually lost when the borrower stops paying).
- The distribution of financed amounts (a 200-unit phone and a 2,000-unit appliance are different exposures even if the default probability is the same).
- Whether the 40 % approval rate and the mix of products have been stable over the 60,000-loan window, or whether the rulebook was tightened or loosened part-way through.
- The exact fields on the "application form" (I am assuming a handful of structured fields: age, income, employment status, existing credit obligations, product type, amount, etc. — not free text).

The single most important structural fact is the first unknown: **your training sample is the approved half of the population, and you are being asked to score the whole population.** Every plan must confront that.

---

# Approaches you could take, and what each costs and gives

**A. Train a model on the 60,000 approved loans and deploy it as-is.**
This is the path management is imagining: fit a classifier, plug it in, approve more. It is fast (a week of work) and cheap. What it gives you is a ranking *within* the historically approved population. It cannot tell you that a 25-year-old with no bureau history and a high debt load is riskier than the rulebook thinks, because nobody like that was ever approved to observe. The result will over-approve and the loss curve will surprise you in quarter two. I would not recommend this as the end state, but a version of it (see plan below) is a necessary building block.

**B. Add a "rejection-inference" step so the model sees the full applicant population.**
You already have the rejected applications' features. You can fit a second, small model on the *combined* approved-plus-rejected sample whose only job is to predict *was this application approved under the old rulebook?* Call it the selection model. You then use it to re-weight the 60,000 approved loans so that, in the re-weighted sample, the feature distribution matches the full applicant pool rather than just the approved slice. The risk model is then trained on those re-weighted approved loans. This is a standard correction (sometimes called Heckman-style or two-phase rejection inference).
- *Cost:* moderate modelling effort; you need to handle the fact that the selection model itself is estimated from finite data, so the re-weights have uncertainty. It is most reliable when the rulebook is mostly deterministic (a scorecard cutoff) rather than a tangle of interacting rules, because then the selection model is well-specified.
- *Give:* a risk estimate that is much less biased for the "would-have-been-rejected" region. You can start to approve people the old rules excluded, with a calibrated sense of their default probability.

**C. Run a small controlled experiment: approve a random slice of would-be rejections.**
For one to two product cycles (say, three months), you override the rulebook for a small, randomised fraction of applications that the rulebook would have declined, and you actually lend. You then observe their 12-month outcomes.
- *Cost:* you take on real credit loss on those loans; you need a legal and operational process to override the rulebook on a randomised basis without creating a fairness or regulatory issue; you need at least one full 12-month maturation window before you have clean outcome data, so the first usable data arrive roughly a year after you start.
- *Give:* the gold-standard, unbiased outcome labels for the rejection region. This is the only way to *know* rather than *infer* the risk of people the rulebook never approved. It also gives you a clean A/B comparison: rulebook-approved vs. model-approved.
- *Practical note:* you do not need to wait for this to build the first model. You can build and deploy on the rejection-inference estimate (approach B) now, and let the experiment's outcomes arrive later to retrain and validate.

**D. Refine the existing rulebook with a few more variables and tighter segmentation.**
No machine learning per se. You segment the 60,000 loans by a handful of strong predictors (bureau score band, product type, LTV, months since last delinquency) and look at observed default rates in each cell. You adjust the approval thresholds per cell.
- *Cost:* low. A spreadsheet or a basic decision-tree fit.
- *Give:* a modest, explainable improvement. You will nudge the approval rate up a few points and cut a bit of loss. You will *not* unlock the same growth a well-built model can, because you are still trapped inside the rulebook's feature space and its binary logic. This is a reasonable fallback or a sanity-check baseline, not the end game.

**E. A gradient-boosted tree (XGBoost / LightGBM) vs. a regularised logistic-regression scorecard, as the core risk model.**
Both can be trained on the re-weighted sample from approach B.
- *Gradient-boosted trees:* typically a few points higher AUC on tabular data; capture interactions you would not think to hand-code (e.g., "young + no bureau + high-debt + appliance = high risk"). Cost: you need a SHAP or similar layer to produce per-decision explanations for audit; the model is a black box to a non-technical regulator unless you wrap it. Deployment latency at the counter is fine (a few dozen trees score in milliseconds).
- *Logistic-regression scorecard:* every coefficient is a story you can tell the regulator and the sales floor. It is easier to monitor, easier to explain, and more stable when the data shifts slightly. Cost: it will underfit if the true risk surface has strong interactions; you may need to hand-craft interaction terms.
- For a shop-counter consumer-lending context where explainability and regulatory comfort matter, I would lean toward the logistic-regression scorecard *as the production model* and use the gradient-boosted tree as an internal benchmark to check that the scorecard is not leaving material risk on the table.

# The plan I would follow, in order

**Step 1 – Get the data and understand the rulebook (this week, parallel to the export).**
- Export the 60,000 approved loans and the rejected applications. Confirm the fields, their types, and missing-value patterns. Confirm the 12-month default label: is it "ever 30+ days past due" or "charge-off"? The two give different targets.
- Sit with the underwriters who wrote the rulebook and get the rules in executable form (a pseudo-code or a simple script). You need to know, for any given feature vector, whether the rulebook would have approved or declined. This is what lets you build the selection model and also lets you check the rulebook's logic for gaps.
- *What this needs:* the exported data, access to the underwriters, a day or two of cleaning.
- *How you check it:* run the rulebook script on the 60,000 and confirm it reproduces "approved" for all of them; run it on the rejected set and confirm it reproduces "declined." If it does not, there are missing rules or data-entry quirks to fix before anything else.

**Step 2 – Build the selection model (rejection-inference correction).**
- Pool the 60,000 approved and the rejected applications. The label is 1 = approved, 0 = rejected. Fit a logistic regression (or a shallow tree if the rulebook is very non-linear) predicting that label from the shared features (form fields + bureau score).
- For each of the 60,000 approved loans, compute the predicted P(approved) from the selection model. The inverse-probability weight is 1 / P(approved) for that row. Loans that the rulebook approved "easily" (high P(approved)) get low weight; loans near the rulebook's rejection boundary get higher weight, pulling the effective training distribution toward the full applicant pool.
- *What this needs:* the combined dataset, a few hours of modelling.
- *How you check it:* the selection model should fit the known rulebook well (high accuracy on a hold-out slice of the combined data, since the rulebook is deterministic). The re-weighted feature distributions should look closer to the full applicant pool than to the approved-only pool. You should inspect the weight distribution for extreme values and cap them (e.g., at the 99th percentile) to avoid one odd loan dominating the fit.

**Step 3 – Build the risk model on the re-weighted approved loans.**
- Train the core model (logistic-regression scorecard as the production candidate; gradient-boosted tree as the benchmark) to predict 12-month default, using the inverse-probability weights from Step 2.
- Use a **time-based split**, not a random split: the most recent, say, 20 % of loans (by disbursement date) are your test set, because the model will be applied to *future* applicants and you want to test against the most recent risk environment.
- *What this needs:* the re-weighted dataset, the time split, a day or two of tuning (regularisation, feature selection).
- *How you check it:* on the test slice, look at (a) discrimination (AUC, KS statistic), (b) **calibration** — if the model says 8 %, do roughly 8 % of that bin actually default within 12 months? Calibration matters more than AUC here, because the threshold you set will be read as "this person has a 10 % chance of defaulting," and that number must be credible. (c) Segment-level lift: does the model separate the top risk decile from the bottom better than the old rulebook does?

**Step 4 – Set the decision threshold and the business case.**
- The model outputs a probability for each applicant. You, as credit risk manager, choose the cut-off: "approve if P(default) < X." The cut-off is **not** determined by the model; it is a business decision that balances expected loss against the lost revenue of a declined sale.
- Using the re-weighted model and the full applicant pool (approved + rejected features), you can estimate, for any candidate cut-off, the projected approval rate and the projected weighted-expected-loss. Present management a small table: "at cut-off X we approve Y % and expect Z basis-points of loss; at cut-off X+we approve Y+ % and expect Z+ bps." Let them pick the risk appetite.
- *What this needs:* the probability model, the full applicant-pool feature distribution, the LGD assumption (get it from collections/charge-off history), the average financed amount by product.
- *How you check it:* the projected numbers must be internally consistent — the expected loss at the new cut-off should be lower than or equal to what you would get by simply approving everyone. If the model's calibration is off, this step is meaningless, so you go back to Step 3.

**Step 5 – Shadow run before the switch.**
- For two to four weeks, run the model in parallel with the rulebook. Every application is scored by both; the **rulebook** still makes the live decision. You log the model's score and what it *would* have decided.
- At the end, compare: on the applications the rulebook approved, does the model's risk ranking make sense? On the applications the rulebook declined, what does the model say? Flag any application where the two systems disagree by more than a material margin and review it manually.
- *What this needs:* the scoring service deployed to the shop-counter system in a read-only or shadow mode, a dashboard logging both decisions, a few analysts to review discrepancies.
- *How you check it:* no systematic bias in one direction; no segment of applicants (e.g., a particular product, a particular shop region) where the model is clearly miscalibrated; latency at the counter is within the operational budget (you mentioned "at the shop counter," which I read as needing the score in seconds, not minutes — confirm the IT team's requirement).

**Step 6 – Go live with a guardrail, then launch the controlled experiment.**
- Switch the live decision to the model, but keep the old rulebook as a **guardrail**: if the model would approve someone the rulebook would decline (or vice-versa) and the probability is in a narrow grey band near the cut-off, route to a human underwriter for a fast manual decision. This catches the model's worst errors in the early weeks without blocking the counter.
- Simultaneously, begin the small randomised experiment (approach C): for a modest fraction of applications the model would decline, approve them at a capped amount so you collect outcome data on the rejection region. This gives you the unbiased 12-month labels you are currently missing.
- *What this needs:* operational change-management (train the sales floor, update the shop system), a risk committee sign-off, a legal/regulatory review of the automated decisioning and of the experiment, a monitoring dashboard.
- *How you check it:* in the first 30 days, compare the model's predicted default rate against the realised early-payment performance (delinquency at 30, 60, 90 days) in the live book. If the realised early delinquency is materially above the model's prediction, tighten the threshold or investigate.

**Step 7 – Monitor, retrain, and expand.**
- Track monthly: approval rate, 30/60/90-day delinquency by model-score bucket, bureau-score distribution drift, product-mix shift. Set alert thresholds.
- When the controlled experiment matures (you have a full 12-month outcome for that random slice), retrain the risk model using those real rejection-region outcomes. This replaces the rejection-inference estimate with observed data and should sharpen the model, especially in the tail.
- Revisit the threshold with management every quarter or when the product mix shifts materially.
- *Stop condition:* if, after the experiment retrain, the model's calibration and discrimination on the new data are within an acceptable band of the shadow-run numbers, and the live performance is tracking the forecast, the project is complete and you are in a steady monitoring cycle. If the model is not materially better than the refined rulebook (approach D), say so to management and recommend keeping the rulebook with targeted tweaks rather than a full replacement.

# What I assumed and what you told me

**You told me:** the 40 % approval rate, the ~60,000 approved loans, the 12-month default label, the existence of rejected applications with form + bureau score but no outcome, the shop-counter real-time setting, and management's growth mandate.

**I assumed (please correct if wrong):**
- The "application form" contains a modest set of structured fields (demographics, income, employment, existing obligations, product type, amount), not free text or images. If there is unstructured data, the feature-engineering step grows.
- The 12-month default label is a single binary flag, not a loss amount. If you have partial-recovery or LGD data per loan, the target should ideally be weighted by loss, not just 0/1.
- The rulebook is a deterministic, knowable set of rules (not a human judgment with undocumented overrides). If underwriters exercise discretion beyond the written rules, the selection model in Step 2 will be noisier.
- The bureau score is a single number from one bureau, not multiple scores or a full bureau report with sub-scores and history. If you have more bureau detail, include it; it will help.
- The 60,000 loans span a reasonable time window (not a single promotional month) and include both phones and appliances.
- Regulatory environment: I assumed the jurisdiction permits algorithmic credit decisions with an explanation requirement (as in most major markets). If there is a specific regulatory constraint on model type or on the experiment, flag it and we adjust Step 5 and 6.

None of the numbers I have used in this plan (the 20 % test-split, the two-to-four-week shadow period, the "grey band" width) are facts about your business; they are starting points to be calibrated to your volume, your product cycle, and your risk tolerance. You have not given me your current loss rate, your LGD, your average ticket size, or your capital constraint, and I would not guess at them. Bring those into the Step 4 conversation and the threshold table will be concrete.

The one number I will hold you to is the selection-bias problem. If you skip Step 2 and go straight from the 60,000 approved loans to a deployed model, you will approve more people, and the loss will come back to you in the second quarter with a lag that makes it look like a market shock rather than a modelling error. The rejection-inference step (or, better, the controlled experiment feeding in later) is what turns "approve more" from a hope into a measured, defensible decision.
